panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Frontal clinical photograph of a 3.5-year-old girl with NBS demonstrating the disease's characteristic facial dysmorphism explicitly captioned as such (microcephaly, sloping forehead, small nose, receding chin, large ears). b: Profile clinical photograph of the same 3.5-year-old girl with NBS, showing the captioned profile dysmorphism (sloping forehead, prominent midface, receding mandible, relatively large ears).
panels.attribution_text: Chrzanowska et al. Nijmegen breakage syndrome (NBS).. Orphanet journal of rare diseases 2012. doi:10.1186/1750-1172-7-13. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (a, b). Facial phenotype in NBS: face (a) and profile (b) of a girl aged 3.5 years. Note microcephaly, sloping forehead, small nose, receding chin, and relatively large ears.
in_text_mentions: The dysmorphic facial features are very similar among all patients with NBS and become more obvious with age. The prominent midface is emphasized by the sloping forehead and the receding mandible, which seems to be secondary to the underdevelopment of the cranium (Figure 1a, b). Other facial characteristics are more subtle and diverse, i.e. palpebral fissures are upwardly slanted in most patients, and the shape of the nose may be both long and beaked as well as upturned with anteverted nostrils. In individual patients, cleft lip/palate or choanal atresia have also been described [3].

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a patient with genetically/ethically anonymized (black-barred) eyes; caption and in-text description explicitly attribute the microcephaly and typical bird-like facial appearance (prominent midface, large ears) to the patient with Nijmegen breakage syndrome, whose article title and primary disease is Nijmegen breakage syndrome. Findings map to the allowed vocabulary; hypertelorism and upward-slanting palpebral fissures are described in text but absent from the vocabulary, so proposed. Skin tone judged from visible, evenly lit monochrome facial skin (appears light); age group supported by in-text pediatric anthropometrics (height 129 cm, weight 29 kg).
panels.attribution_text: Pasic et al. Nijmegen breakage syndrome and chronic polyarthritis.. Italian journal of pediatrics 2013. doi:10.1186/1824-7288-39-59. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Microcephaly and typical bird-like appearance in our patient.
in_text_mentions: igation of repeated lung infections. Physical examination on admission included: height, 129 cm (p50) and the body weight, 29 kg (p50); microcephaly (head circumference = 46 cm, < p3); typical facial features with prominent midface, large ears and hyperthelorism with upward slant of the palpebral fissures (Figure 1); hypopigmented spots on trunk and extremities; bilateral clinodactyly and syndactyly of the second and third toe were observed. Chest examination revealed bilateral basilar crackles due to bronchiectasis. Neurological examination and ophtalmologic slit-lamp examination were normal.

Furthermore, the middle phalanx of the little finger of both hands was found to be short (Figure 2c).

The caption describes pleomorphic tumor cells with vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli, and in-text mentions Reed-Sternberg cells, supporting the NBS vocabulary finding lymphoma_histology. Disease attribution is supported by the disease-focused article title and in-text case details. No skin is shown, so skin tone is null. Scale bar is present.

CD19, CD22, CD43, CD45, and ALK were negative. CD10 stain was predominately negative and testing for cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus were negative. MRI of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was used for staging of disease and showed lymphadenopathy of the lesser sac and gastric cardia (Fig. 6). Attribution rests on the disease-focused article title plus the specific captioned nodal mass rather than a general mention, but because the nodal disease is the lymphoma complication of NBS, confidence is moderate. Annotations (measurement text and arrow) are present; no skin is shown, so skin tone is null and ethnicity is not stated.

panels.rationale: Single-image immunohistochemistry panel from a patient with Nijmegen breakage syndrome and primary gastric Hodgkin lymphoma. The article title and in-text mention directly link the lymphoma to Nijmegen breakage syndrome, and the panel shows CD30-positive lymphoma histology, a recognized NBS-associated manifestation. The case is described as rare, so typicality is atypical.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Clinical photo of a granulomatous skin lesion in a boy with Nijmegen breakage syndrome (caption explicitly states NBS). The manifestation is an autoimmune complication reported in NBS, though not among the vocabulary findings; proposed findings capture the visible lesion. B: Clinical photo of the same granulomatous lesion after conditioning for HSCT in a boy with NBS. It is a real patient image showing the manifestation, though post-treatment, so slightly lower confidence. C: H&E histology of skin from the NBS patient showing mixed-cell infiltrate in superficial and deep dermis, corresponding to the granulomatous lesion. Disease attribution from caption/in-text; findings not in vocabulary are proposed. D: Higher-magnification H&E histology from the NBS patient showing palisaded inflammatory infiltrate with histiocytes, lymphocytes, neutrophils, and basophilic collagen changes. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Frontal facial view of genetically confirmed NBS patient in NBS-focused case report captioned 'Facial features of our patient'; shows characteristic NBS facies with sloping forehead and receding mandible visually, plus periorbital lesion noted in-text. B: Lateral facial view of same genetically confirmed NBS patient; shows sloping forehead and receding mandible profile characteristic of NBS facies, with periorbital squamous lesion described in-text.
